title: Japanese Fir: Ancient Japanese Firs You Can Visit
meta_description: None of the three carries a recorded age, since Japan's giant-tree register measures girth, not years. Three Japanese firs mapped around Higashi-Hiroshima.
intro: Momi, the Japanese fir, is a warm-temperate species of Honshu and Kyushu that favours cool upland shrine groves and dislikes heat. All three the site maps grow within a few kilometres of each other around Higashi-Hiroshima's Toyosaka hills, and none carries a recorded age: Japan's giant-tree register measures girth, not years. Uneyama Shrine's fir, at 3.4 metres, stands in a grove the prefecture designated in 1987 and later lost trees to a typhoon; written accounts of the grove name five other species and never this one. Hongu Hachiman's fir, also 3.4 metres, shares its hilltop with cedars by the dozen and a 1701 hall the city protects as an important cultural property. Behind Morimasa Shrine stands the smallest of the three, exactly three metres round in the 2000 survey, which is to say it qualified for the register by nothing at all.
